title: Beige Book — September 2, 2026 (Chicago District and national)
summary: Chicago District: Economic activity in the Seventh District increased slightly in July and early August, and contacts expected a similar pace of increase over the next 12 months. Manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment was up slightly; consumer spending and construction and real estate activity were flat on balance; business spending declined slightly; and nonbusiness contacts saw no change in economic activity. Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened slightly. Farm income expectations for 2026 improved some. National: Economic activity increased modestly since early July. Ten of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported growth in the slight to moderate range; two Districts reported no change. Consumer spending grew slightly on balance; reports reflected both heightened price sensitivity on the one hand and solid high-end purchases on the other. Auto sales were mostly subdued, dampened by downbeat consumer confidence, high fuel prices, and rising financing costs. Tourism activity increased. Notably, airlines reported strong demand despite higher airfares. Manufacturing activity picked up across most Districts, with some highlighting ongoing strength in demand for defense and data center-related orders. Services firms reported slight to modest increases in activity. Financial conditions improved slightly as loan volumes remained solid or increased across most Districts. Residential construction declined while nonresidential construction increased on balance, with some Districts noting a high concentration of activity related to data center projects. Agriculture conditions saw slight improvement but generally remained strained; the livestock sector was strong while conditions were stressed among crop producers. The general outlook for the coming months was positive, but sentiment was mixed across sectors, with contacts reporting heightened uncertainty surrounding the effects of higher energy prices, policy, and international conflict.

title: Beige Book — October 14, 2026 (Chicago District and national)
summary: Chicago District: Economic activity in the Seventh District was flat on balance in late August and September, and contacts expected a slight pace of increase in the coming year. Manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment was up slightly; consumer spending was flat on balance; construction and real estate activity and business spending declined slightly; and nonbusiness contacts saw no change in economic activity. Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened modestly. Farm income expectations for 2026 were down slightly. National: Since the prior Beige Book, two of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported moderate growth in economic activity. Three Districts reported modest growth, while four reported slight growth, and three reported no significant change. Robust, broad-based growth in manufacturing led the moderate growth reported in the Dallas District. While not as robust, another six Districts reported modest to moderate growth from their manufacturing firms. The remaining five Districts noted little or no manufacturing growth. Reports on other sectors indicate little growth overall. Most Districts reported little or no change in overall consumer spending. Auto contacts noted flat to modestly lower sales in five of the six Districts that reported. Over half of the Districts noted that consumer spending was driven by high-income households. Even in Dallas, where District firms reported solid retail sales, there were "some reports of lower-income customers being more cautious with spending." Tourism continued to grow, but firms in the Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco Districts noted a decline in sales from Canadian tourists. Overall, most Districts reported that firms have maintained a positive economic outlook for the coming months. However, expectations tend to be for slight growth, weighted toward manufacturing and burdened by persistent uncertainties.

title: Beige Book — November 25, 2026 (Chicago District and national)
summary: Chicago District: Economic activity in the Seventh District was unchanged overall in October and early November, similar to the assessment in the prior reporting period. Contacts expected a slight decrease over the coming year. Manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment was up slightly; consumer spending was flat on balance; construction and real estate activity and business spending declined modestly; and nonbusiness contacts saw no change in economic activity. Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened modestly. Farm income expectations for 2026 edged lower. National: Eight of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported growth in the slight to moderate range, while four Districts reported no change. Consumer spending was little changed, as households remained price sensitive and were increasingly selective in discretionary purchases. Tourism and travel activity was solid while entertainment and hospitality spending was mixed overall. Auto sales softened, which contacts attributed to elevated fuel prices and higher interest rates. Residential real estate activity weakened as affordability challenges suppressed demand, while commercial real estate activity was mixed. Construction activity declined amid higher borrowing costs and elevated construction costs. Manufacturing activity grew modestly overall, as robust demand in several industrial segments offset weakness in consumer-facing and housing-related goods. Overall transportation activity grew modestly despite uneven demand, persistent capacity and infrastructure constraints, and rising cost pressures. Port volumes were slightly lower due to weather-driven disruptions, even as data center–related imports rose. Energy activity grew modestly but investment in this sector remained restrained by elevated geopolitical, policy, and cost uncertainties. Banking conditions were little changed overall, as loan demand remained subdued, while nonfinancial services activity increased slightly. High costs for housing and other essentials strained household budgets, increased demand for social services, and stretched nonprofit capacity. Overall, the majority of Districts expected slight to moderate growth.
